speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF EUROPEAN CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of the recognized interest of many members, together with the interest of the livestock people involved, I would like to advise the House that permits providing for this year's importation of European cattle will be issued within the next ten to fifteen days.
As was the case last year, it is expected that 615 head of cattle can be imported from France and Switzerland this year and discussions are progressing aimed at establishing satisfactory veterinary agreements with some other European countries, including Italy.
As in the past years, many more applications were received than can be accommodated within our maximum security quarantine facilities. More than 1,200 people asked for authority to import approximately 7,000 head of cattle.
Each application must be supported by a project proposal indicating the purpose to which the imported cattle are to be put, and a committee of four geneticists then examines these project proposals advising the department on which, in their view, would contribute most to the development of the livestock industry in Canada. The permits are then issued on the basis of this priority rating given by the genetic committee.
Because applications for permits are assessed upon the basis of breeding projects, stipulating particular breeds, those receiving import permits will be restricted to purchasing the breed designated in their project proposals.
Export restrictions against imported animals will be eased this year. Many Charolais animals imported in 1966-67 have made their contribution to developing this breed in Canada and it is now felt that up to 50 per cent of these animals, which have been in Canada for at least 36 months, can now be released from the embargo.

I would have been pleased if the minister had also stated what is being done about a problem that is now blowing up in the United States. It was stated on the CBC farm broadcast today that United States cattlemen are pressing for import quotas on the shipment of Canadian beef into the United States because Canada is allowing so much Australian and New Zealand beef to be trans-shipped through Canada to the United States. If our imports into the United States are restricted, we may bring in as many high quality breeding animals from Europe as we like but our price structure will decline and our marketing problems will increase.
I urge the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Agriculture to announce to the House before it rises what they are going to do about the situation that is now building up because importation of beef from New Zealand and Australia has been encouraged. When I asked a question I was told that it was mostly processing beef. It is not processing beef and it is not processing
(Mr. Muir (Lisgar).]
beef when it passes through Canada on the way to the United States market.

subtopic: STATEMENT ON IMPORTATION OF EUROPEAN CATTLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has just announced that permits will be issued to authorize the importation into Canada of cattle from Europe in order to promote their breeding here. To my mind, the minister should also give particular attention to Canadian breeds of horses and cattle.
At the present time, the emphasis is on European imports. The minister does not seem to know that the Canadian government has refused to keep at the Ottawa experimental farm the only cross-bred stock of the last 75 years.
In fact, horses and cattle of Canadian stock have no place in Canada today. This stock is indigenous to our country and today Canadian breeders are compelled to pay the costs of breeding and of advertising outside the country.
I suggest that the minister is well-advised to give Canadian breeders the opportunity to obtain specimens of European stocks, but, in co-operation with the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the minister should give particular attention to our own Canadian cattle and horses, unkown in other countries and for which there is great demand. Unfortunately, breeders must themselves pay the costs of advertising and transport when they take part in shows in South America and elsewhere, where this stock is unkown. The Department of Agriculture could do much to develop trade in this field, especially in Canadian cattle and horses.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a motion to make under the terms of Standing Order 43 which Your Honour will recall requires unanimous consent before it can be put. I would hope that the Prime Minister, in his wish to see matters conducted expeditiously, can muzzle the more negative members of his cabinet and permit the motion to be put.
A recent report entitled "Death of a Delta", prepared by the University of Alberta resources committee and presented to the gov-
June 25, 1970	COMMONS
ernments of Canada and Alberta, has underlined the extreme seriousness of the reduced level of the Peace River following construction of the Bennett Dam. When the Liberal government betrayed the long-range interest of the north by allowing the British Columbia government to construct this dam without any protection under the Navigable Waters Protection Act or otherwise, the present situation became inevitable.
For at least two years the level of the Peace has been down, endangering water supplies to municipalities. The present report emphasizes the immense danger to the ecology of the area between the Peace and the Athabasca and the very likely effect on the McKenzie and the Great Slave Lake water system. Wildlife, transportation and the livelihood of people are all at stake.
Finally, our failure to deal with this problem makes our grandiose proposals to safeguard the far north something of a mockery and is bound to adversely affect our efforts to persuade the United States and other nations that we have any genuine concern for the north.
I would therefore move the following motion, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward Hastings (Mr. Hees), if unanimous consent is given:
That the report of the University of Alberta resources centre be forthwith referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development for study and report before the end of this session, and that the representatives of the government appear before the committee to indicate the position of the government of Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely, the new situation created by the acceleration and spread of the rotational strikes by postal employees, thus creating a new threat of a nation-wide postal strike, the failure of the Treasury Board to negotiate a settlement to end the disruption of postal services, and the urgent need to debate the serious situation before the House adjourns for the summer recess.

maintopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE ACCELERATED DISRUPTION OF SERVICE-FAILURE TO NEGOTIATE SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask leave to move the adjournment of the House under Standing Order 26. The matter is the disruption of the postal service, the indication that a more serious abridgement of normal delivery service is contemplated, and the failure of the negotiators to make progress toward a settlement of the dispute. In the face of such a serious diminution of an important service to which the Canadian public are entitled and the expected early adjournment of the House for the summer recess, I believe it is of urgent public importance that this House discuss this serious matter of public interest.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MOTIONS TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26 POST OFFICE ACCELERATED DISRUPTION OF SERVICE-FAILURE TO NEGOTIATE SETTLEMENT OF DISPUTE
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, both the hon. member for York South and the hon. member for Hillsborough have filed the notice

required by Standing Order 26. All hon. members will recognize the importance of the situation alluded to in the proposed motions. Indeed, on a number of occasions during the last month or so the suggestion has been made that there should be an emergency debate under Standing Order 26 for the purpose of discussing the postal situation. It might well be argued that this fact alone or in itself would preclude the holding of a special debate since we are dealing essentially with a continuing situation. On the other hand, both hon. members have presented the argument that there has been a change in the situation, in particular an acceleration in the rotational strikes by postal employees, and they have alluded also to the fact that the House is likely to adjourn within the next few days.
Because of the very special circumstances it may well be that hon. members would want to agree that an opportunity be provided for such a debate before the summer recess. Since there will have to be some measure of planning and consultation between House Leaders for the orderly conduct of parliamentary business during the days ahead, I would hesitate to propose to the House a debate under Standing Order 26 without further consideration and consultation with the House Leaders.
In view of all these circumstances I propose, under the provisions of section 6 of Standing Order 26, to defer my decision until later in this sitting.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Prime Minister.
Yesterday, a grievous event occurred in the national capital: a bomb blast killed one person. Could the Prime Minister tell us if, in order to facilitate the inquiry now going on,

June 25, 1970
Inquiries of the Ministry he intends to offer, as did the province of Quebec, a reward to those who could give information leading to the arrest of the persons responsible for the bombing?

Kon. John N. Turner (Minister of Justice):
Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I might be allowed to reply on behalf of the Prime Minister and on behalf of the Solicitor General. I think the bombing yesterday was a savage, cowardly and insane act.

maintopic: LEADING TO ARREST OF THOSE RESPONSIBLE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: LEADING TO ARREST OF THOSE RESPONSIBLE
speechtext:
I am sure all members of the House share my feeling of outrage. An innocent woman, Madame Jeanne D'Arc St.-Germain, was killed by the blast and two other employees were injured. On behalf of the government and I am sure on behalf of all members of the House I want to express to the family of Madame St.-Germain our deepest sympathy.
Yesterday the Minister of National Defence visited the site personally. Later in the day I visited the site of the blast accompanied by the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and by Mr. Ken Fogarty, the Mayor of Ottawa. We inspected the damage and received a report on the progress of the investigation. As a matter of fact, I spoke to Corporal Vallance who was on duty less than eight feet from the site of the blast at the time the blast occurred but who miraculously survived except for a few cuts.
The investigation of this incident is being carried out by the Ottawa City Police at the present time with the full assistance and cooperation of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Canadian Forces Military Police, investigation section, and the Ontario Fire Marshal's office. In respect of the specific question may I say that I have had informal discussions with the Attorney General of Ontario and the Mayor of Ottawa concerning the possibility of a reward. The government, however, wants to consider the answer to this question in light of the progress of the investigation. I want to assure the hon. member and the House that we will do everything necessary to push this investigation to a successful conclusion.

When I moved this amendment initially, I stated quite clearly that I was not absolutely married to its wording and contents. I was attempting to make the point that electors in urban polling divisions whose names did not appear on the list should have an opportunity to cast their ballots on election day after being vouched for by someone else.
It was then brought to my attention that the fount of all good things resides in Nova Scotia-I might accept that notion except to the extent that it relates to the fishing industry-and that the elections act of that province provides a way of enabling this objective to be realized. I was not, myself, familiar with the legislation but I understand it has worked fairly well. It may, therefore, provide a basis for an alternative suggestion. If the idea seems to gain some acceptance we might stand the clause before us now, together with the proposed amendment, to see whether or not we could develop something in the interim which would be satisfactory.
Under the Nova Scotia act, to recapitulate, a revising officer in cities or town having a population of more than 5,000 is authorized to sit on ordinary polling days at the headquarters of the returning officer. This official may be approached by a person who is qualified to vote and whose name is not on the list. After swearing an oath he is given a certificate which he takes to the polling station, accompanied by another person whose name is on the list for that polling division. The latter vouches for him and he is then able to cast his ballot. I agree there may be difficulties in very large communities in connection with this procedure since it might be impracticable for people to travel long distances to the office of the returning officer, but this is not an insurmountable problem.
If the procedure I have outlined seems to be a more practical way of affording those whose

The suggestion made by the hon. member for Skeena has some appeal to me. I shall not repeat the points I made when the committee last sat with regard to the Nova Scotia procedure, but if the President of the Privy Council would agree to stand this clause we would welcome any change which might extend this privilege to the electors, making sure that all voters may exercise their franchise as far as lies within our power.

The necessity for this amendment is not apparent, but according to the law officers of the Crown it should be made in order to prevent contestations or litigation in the future. It is consequential to the one that was adopted Tuesday night.

Mr. Chairman, I had a brief opportunity to look at this amendment and, initially, I did not have any difficulty when attempting to ascertain why this was necessary. As I understand it, subsection (2) of 21, which is sought to be amended here, contains the saving feature about ineligible 
candidates. Clause 21 provides that certain persons are not eligible to be candidates, and subsclause 2 says that the application of subclause 1 shall not render certain other people ineligible. I presume here that some difficulty might arise. Again, I might point out that one needs a few moments to follow this.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
For the sake of argument, suppose a person should be found guilty of a corrupt practice and thus declared ineligible for a period of five years next after the date of his being so found, reported, declared guilty and so on. Would this declaration override that provision, as would paragraph (g) of subclause 2 which relates to employees in the public service or paragraph (f) which concerns members of the reserve forces? I realize that one is not supposed to ask, nor is a minister of the Crown supposed to give, legal opinions about matters but I believe there must be an exception in this case bceause we are dealing with a bill that is above and beyond government policy. It relates to the right of people to choose candidates. Without having had more than just a moment or two to read the amendment and lit it into clause 21 of the bill, this thought immediately came to mind. Mr. Chairman, I have not written an amendment in respect of this clause but it would be easy to do so. This relates to the matters that were put before the committee when we were dealing with the clause concerning the time during which the polls would be open on election day.
As hon. members will recall, I raised the question concerning loggers on Vancouver Island, and in other parts of British Columbia, who may spend up to two or two and a half
June 25, 1970

hours getting from their place of work to their place of residence which of course would be where they would vote. A slight difficulty like a flat tire or difficulty in respect of the "crummy", the bus which brings them back into work, could under some circumstances mean they would not get back home in time to vote because of this three-hour provision. If, for argument's sake, the polls closed at eight o'clock by virtue of the daylight saving time provisions and the employee was permitted three consecutive hours free from his employment in order to vote, and this period of three consecutive hours started at four o'clock, under the circumstances which I related he would have three hours in which to get from his place of work to the polls to vote. I wonder whether there would be a disposition to make a change in this provision. Initially, I put this proposition forward as a suggestion, but I am fully prepared to move an amendment if there should be general agreement to the idea that we change the three consecutive hours to four consecutive hours in order to take account of this situation. Mr. Chairman, my remarks on this clause probably lead into the short general comment I wish to make on third reading of the bill, namely, the necessity to engage in sort of an educational program in order to acquaint people with the provisions of the law. The earlier section gives some direction to the voter by saying that he shall proceed into the compartment and, if I recall the words, with the black lead pencil provided therein mark his ballot, perhaps it even says "with an X or a cross". (b) it has been marked with a writing instrument other than a black lead pencil or with a mark other than a cross, if the mark does not constitute identification of the elector.
I appreciate that it would be difficult to give instructions to the elector to mark the ballot with any kind of instrument he likes. This would be inviting trouble. We would have finger prints and I do not know what else indicating the vote on the ballot. But I want to draw to the committee's attention the fact that this provision might create confusion in the minds of the electors and certainly will create confusion in the minds of the deputy returning officers and poll clerks. For many years, both under the provincial and federal law, these people have been used to the idea that a ballot can only be marked by a cross made with a pencil. On election night, therefore, if someone marks a tick with a red pen, for argument's sake, there might be a big argument. The ballot might be invalidated because it was marked that way, not taking into account the fact that it may be identifying the elector.

This tendency to discuss becomes contagious. I said earlier how much I was indebted to the hon. member for Leeds who sold me on the broadminded attitude toward marking the ballot. As I was saying at an earlier stage, this in fact should be called a Code amendment. I do think that it is extremely important that we try somehow- and this will come up later-to get across an educative process. 1 regret to say that in the six parliaments I have served I have not seen a measure of such public importance as this one so poorly and inadequately reported by the press of the country, so it will be all the more necessary that something be done.

I have a small amendment to clause 52. I propose that it be amended by adding a new subclause (3) which reads as follows:

Without going into it too deeply, may I explain that this is simply to add a further measure of protection to the secrecy of the franchise of the voters under the special voting rules, that is to say, the Canadian armed forces voters. We have taken substantial steps to try to protect the secrecy of their franchise in the amendments we made to this bill, and this is just one minor addition. speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre indicated, I was very sympathetic to the notion of the somewhat broader proposition that he had put, namely that the election reporting system
June 25, 1970

should be structured in such a way that not only on voting night but even in the blue book which results ultimately from the election, there would be no indication to an outside observer of what part of the total of the advance poll and the service vote, was the service vote. He suggested that this should occur in this case just as it does with certain polling divisions which are grouped with larger numbers so as to assure the secrecy of the ballot. I had the opportunity to discuss this at length with those responsible for running the elections, and they pointed out to me the shortcomings of the broader proposition to which, as the hon. member indicated, I had given some approval at second reading.
The procedure, as I understand it, is as follows. The returning officer will be receiving from each of the advance polls a ballot box with the ballots in it, and for the purposes of controlling the legitimacy of the vote at each of those advance polling stations the ballot box is counted by itself. Then, the advance poll is the aggregate of each of the individual counts from those ballot boxes. That ballot box is opened and counted in the presence, not only of the chief returning officer and his clerk, but also in the presence of such representatives as the parties want to appoint.
The service ballot is handled in a somewhat different manner. This is where a further difficulty arises. It is not the same type of ballot as the other. What had appealed to me was the possibility of working on a system whereby all the ballots might be so intermingled that in the actual act of counting it would be impossible to differentiate. So far as the service ballot is concerned, it is not the standard ballot marked with an X or other distinguishing mark opposite the appropriate name but rather a ballot on which the name of the candidate selected is written in. So there are two different types of ballot, and the intermingling proposition would not work. What we have, therefore, for reasons of security and integrity of the poll as an identification at least for those working inside the returning officer's office is a breakdown as between the advance poll and the service vote because the advance poll has been counted and also because the service vote is a different kind of ballot.
[DOT] (4:10p.m.)
What would happen, therefore, in the case of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is that all people working on the polling staff, including
Canada Elections Act
representatives of the parties, would know what the service vote was. The purpose, in effect, would be to prevent the press from finding out, but they could find out quickly enough by asking around.
By this reasoning, I have been reluctantly forced to the conclusion that this kind of anonymity which I had hoped to give is not possible. It would be possible to put some controls on announcements on election night, I agree, but when the official count is being taken there would be an opportunity for the representatives to check on the advance poll and by the simple process of subtraction to find out the service vote. Under the present system, I do not see how you can ensure this ballot protection.
My understanding is that the member for Dartmouth-Halifax East was rather less ambitious in his amendment. He is really not purporting to give an instruction to anybody who is involved not to reveal what they have seen; he is giving an instruction to the returning officer which is effective only on election night. The instruction to the returning officer is that in announcing the advance poll he will commence it and the service vote together, even though he and some other people will know what the difference is. That seems to me to be a legitimate objective and I would be prepared to accept it. Perhaps it would be only fair to hear what the hon. member would have proposed had he been on his feet first.

Mr. Chairman, my amendment is almost identical to that of the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East. What I said on second reading and at an earlier stage may have been misunderstood because I said it badly. I realized you could not combine these results in the official returns in the blue book, and that they would have to be accounted for in separate ballots in the polls. As I understand the reasoning of the President of the Privy Council, he feels this would not be practical. The armed forces and overseas public service vote will be counted and communicated by the Chief Electoral Officer to each returning officer, so it seems to me it is no problem for the returning officer to hold that result until such time as all results in the advance poll come in. He does not reveal the vote on the advance polls until he has the total count. I assume the advance poll will be counted on the night it is held and the results transmitted to the office of the returning officer. Upon receipt of those results, they will be combined with the results he has received by

June 25, 1970
Canada Elections Act
telephone or telegraph of the armed forces and overseas public service vote, to make one total for each candidate. This is what will be released from the office of the returning officer on election night and thereafter, of course, the advance polls and the polls of the armed forces and overseas public service vote will be separated.
I agree that anonymity should be protected as far as possible on election night, but thereafter it is the same as any other poll. We do not have to worry about identification of groups.
Instead of "at least one of the advance polls" my amendment reads "the total number of votes cast for each candidate in all of the advance polls". In other words, if there were six advance polls there would be one total. The returning officer would release the vote in a manner similar for the advance armed forces and overseas public service vote, so there would be one figure for each candidate. I see no problem here in the light of the mechanism used for counting the advance poll; the kind of ballot surely has nothing to do with this. I think the mechanism can be handled quite well by the returning officer in his office that night.

On clause 53, subclause 7-Application for recount by returning officer.

Mr. Chairman, this clause provides for what can be called an automatic recount. In the case of a tie in the number of votes, instead of the returning officer casting a deciding ballot that night, he shall petition

for a recount. Only after recount, if there is still an equality of votes, will the returning officer cast his deciding ballot. This takes the pressure off the returning officer and it means that the cost of the recount is borne by the Treasury instead of by a candidate who lost by one vote. It does not go quite far enough, however. Everyone will agree that uncertainty and indecision have no place in an election. The electoral process should allow for a recount to be conducted under certain other conditions.
I should like to move that clause 53, subclause 7 be amended by deleting the first paragraph and substituting therefor the following:
Where on the official addition of the votes, there is an equality of votes between two or more candidates and an additional vote for one of such candidates would entitle one of those candidates to he declared as having the largest number of votes, or where on the official addition of votes there is less than 25 votes difference between the candidate having the highest number of votes and any other candidate, the returning officer shall
The intent of this amendment is that where there is a difference between the leading candidate and one or more other candidates of 24 votes or less, the returning officer would automatically petition for a recount. The most obvious reason for this is that the costs of a recount are borne by a candidate and his party. We felt that where the difference was more than 24, the cost should be borne by a candidate and his party. We felt that this was a reasonably low enough figure to allow for a better way of getting the decision confirmed by that recount and could possibly save some time as well. It is almost certain that when a vote is close in any constituency, one or more of the candidates will petition for a recount. If there should be a small difference between the numbers of ballots cast for the leading and second candidates, the process of recounting will be undertaken more quickly. It will be done under the authority of the electoral laws and electoral officers, and you will avoid partisan activities in connection with this matter on the part of one or more of the candidates or political parties. I hope that the members of the committee will agree that this will be an improvement.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Sometimes, when seats are won by a margin of a handful of votes there are arguments and legal proceedings, and unfortunate feelings are sometimes generated in electoral districts while these proceedings are going on.
June 25, 1970

It seems to me that if, instead of petitions on the part of political parties and candidates for a recount, the matter could be undertaken by election officials and the courts, there would be a great improvement in our electoral process. Although the election results might be delayed for a few days, this matter would be much better handled than under our present system. 1 hope this amendment commends itself to the members of the committee.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we will be disposed to accept the amendment. There have been suggested to me a number of drafting changes. We accept the principle and the wording will be almost the same. It is the draftsmen's sense of elegance which dictates this rather than the substance of the amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I have no strenuous objection to this at all. Of course, it puts out of bounds the candidate who, for good and sufficient reasons, does not care for a recount. I remember that in a certain strong Highland section of a certain province a candidate came close to winning, and certain people suggested that he should seek a recount. His response was, "If my people thought I was such a poor sport that I could not win on the hustings and therefore tried to win in the judge's chambers, they would not support me again." He did not have a recount and the next time he won the seat for his party for the first time in 50 years. Of coruse, I do not suggest that as a reason I might be against it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to move an amendment to subclause 1 of clause 62 concerning the legal capacity of one who acts as an official agent. We have already adopted clause 20 saying that a candidate must be 18 years of age or over, and there is no provision in the act regarding the capacity of the official agent to act in certain instances. I can envisage a case where a candidate might be 18 or 19 years old and, in certain instances, he would be somewhat restricted in his legal dealings. He might also have an official agent who might also be 18 or 19 years old, and serious difficulties might arise. I am not as familiar with the laws of other provinces as I am with those of Quebec. May I remind the committee that the official agent is the one who, on behalf of the candidate, engages in contracts for printing, advertising and other matters which involve electoral expenses. If he were to plead his minority in certain instances I can see that difficulties might arise. To prevent these I wish to move the following amendment:
That Bill C-215 be amended by striking out lines 13 to 19 on page 156 and substituting the following: "an official agent
(a)	who shall be a person who is capable of entering into contracts in the province in which the electoral district of the candidate is located, and
(b)	whose name, address and occupation shall be
(i)	declared to the returning officer, in the nomination paper in Form No. 27 by or on behalf of the candidate, on or before nomination day, and
(ii)	published in the Notice of Grant of a Poll in Form No. 32."
I think it will be useful to take the precaution of putting a provision into the Act saying that the official agent is a person who is capable of entering into legal contracts.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)

Mr. Chairman, the last amendment emanating from the founts of legal wisdom got us into a little difficulty. I am concerned about this one. I know what lawyers will probably say. I feel we are

June 25. 1970
Canada Elections Act
moving toward the isolation of the candidate as an infant in the eyes of the law. I wonder if we have to build up this new status for the agent. What do we do about his principal, the candidate? Can the candidate be 18 years of age if the agent must be 21 years of age?
We are in the process of setting up a category of people who will in fact become the fathers of the Elections Act, namely, the new members of the House of Commons. Is it necessary to single out certain people to be in an age category different from that of the candidates? If we allow a candidate to be someone less than 21, he enters into contract control. I think the deposit has a certain legal validity. The candidate is the principal of the agent who has many returns to which he must attest and swear.
I wonder about isolating the agent and requiring more of him in terms of accumulation of years over the candidate. I was proposing later on in the proceedings to move an amendment to delete the requirement that the returning officer be 21. If the end product, the candidate and potential Member of Parliament, can take on all the plenitude of powers which will follow at the age of 18, I wonder why the lesser lights along the way must burn for three extra years. I am not prepared to concede this, Mr. Chairman. It is out of an abundance of caution as to the authority of the federal Parliament in federal elections to infringe upon the unquestioned power of the provinces over contracts. Rather than have some doubt about the matter, it seems desirable to make this kind of change. In this way the outside world, in dealing with a particular campaign, may at least look to one person who can be made legally responsible for the debts in question. I draw the attention of the committee to clause 62, subclause 2:
In the event of the death or legal Incapacity of any official agent, the candidate shall forthwith appoint another official agent-
The same type of amendment would be required in the clause anyway. Eor many years the Canada Elections Act has acknowledged the importance of the official agent as being the one legally responsible. I hazard the opinion that the general principles of principal and agent may not apply to these particular circumstances. This is a rather particular kind of agent whose status is defined by clause 62. Therefore the situation would be, as I stated on second reading, that of caveat vendor, let the seller beware. When he is dealing with the candidate, let the seller beware if the candidate is or is not legally responsible. We are taking a further step here to make sure that in dealing with the official agent, which essentially is the basic form of contracting in an election system, at least one of the persons in the situation should be capable of being held legally responsible.
This probably is true with the law of Ontario. I will not hazard a guess as to the law of other provinces. However, when a minor is a candidate and the agent has reached his majority you do not have the opportunity of suing both principal and agent. You are confined to suing the agent and taking your remedies against him. This is a preferable situation in terms of contracting if one of the two is to be legally responsibile under the law of the province. It is on that basis, to make the new situation consistent with the inhibition under clause 2, that I recommend this amendment to the committee.

There is a certain hazard in trying to pose queries in legal matters when one is a layman and the other is a lawyer. I will exhibit my ignorance as a layman by posing a question to the President of the Privy Council. It is in terms of the extent to which the federal Elections Act may

be able to make incursions into the field of provincial jurisdiction, namely, the making of contracts. It seems that we already do this. At least it appears this way in subclause 7. I presume the contract referred to is what we are talking about. Subclause 7 reads:
A contract whereby any expenses are incurred on account of or in respect of the conduct or management of an election is not enforceable against a candidate unless made by the candidate himself-*
If the candidate is 18 years of age or less than the age of majority in the particular province where he is running and makes a contract related to expenses, which presumably he is legally entitled to do under this Act, then that contract is enforceable against him regardless of whether he is under the age of majority. I wonder if a federal law can go into a field of the province, namely, the making of contracts? It seems that is the case. Why can we not do it in the case of the official agent? Following upon on subclause 7, you cannot draw the official agent or his subagent into it unless they are authorized in writing to enter into such contracts.

Again, in subclause 12 on page 158 we are probably making another invasion of the field of provincial jurisdiction relating to contracts, because we say that all expenses incurred by or on behalf of a candidate in connection with contracts and management of the election shall be paid within 50 days, and so on. In other words, regardless of what the law relating to such contracts in the provinces concerned may say, we insist that payment must be made within 50 days. This is another example of the committee, and presumably, Parliament, exercising jurisdiction as far as federal elections are concerned, and presumably doing so quite properly under the constitution of Canada. If these are valid points I am making-and I do not really know whether they are or not, in a legal sense-then surely we could make certain provisions with regard to contracts entered into by an agent, regardless of his age.

In order to appreciate the point I am making I think it is necessary to consider briefly subclause 1 which we have just passed. Subclause 1 says no one shall offer food, drink or the like, or any money or valuable consideration to anybody in order to induce him to vote or refrain from voting. In other words, no one may bribe people to vote in a certain way or not to vote at all.
However, under subclause 2 we make it permissible to provide, as I understand it, sandwiches, cakes, cookies, non-alcoholic beverages and other light refreshments in an attempt to influence people into voting or refraining from voting. In other words, we say it is permissible to engage in bribery of a sort as long as it involves non-alcoholic beverages, cakes, cookies and light refreshments generally, provided they are supplied by an official agent, by any person other than a candidate or official agent, at his own expense, at a meeting of electors assembled for the purpose of promoting the election of a candidate, or by any person to an election agent at a polling station. The assumption in the first part is that the meeting is held to promote the election of a candidate. It would seem that the provision of coffee, cakes, tea and the like is a necessary extension of the public meeting and the exhortations that would take place at that meeting.

Paragraph (b), which is the one I want to get to, provides that such refreshments can be provided in order to induce people to vote in a certain way or to refrain from voting-in other words, to engage in a legalized sort of bribery at a meeting of electors called for the purpose of promoting a candidate. We carried subclause 1 but subclause 2 makes an exception of non-alcoholic beverages, sandwiches, cakes and cookies that are provided, under paragraph (b), by any person other than a candidate or official agent who at his own expense provides such refreshment at a meeting to promote the election of a candidate. We have recognized that this is a form of bribery, though not quite so underhanded and illegal as we conceded the situation might be as described in subclause 1. By proscribing against this sort of bribery in subclause 1 we have recognized that it might take place, that it does influence people and that it is an illegal and immoral thing to do.
By extending this concept to subclause 2, paragraph (b), we should recognize that without limiting the activities of people other than the candidate or official agent and everyone within the political party, the organization itself which would want to advance the cause of the candidate in question, cakes, cookies and so on would be provided through the official agent. While the official agent is an agent on behalf of a candidate, he is also an agent on behalf of an extension of the political party to which the candidate belongs. This is part of the campaign, and we seek to endorse it by permitting the official agent and those who are identified with the candidate in an open way to engage in this sort of activity in an attempt to convince voters to cast their vote in a certain way.
Once we go beyond this and permit any other person without restriction to provide refreshment, we are overstepping the bounds of the sort of ethics we want to see contained in the Elections Act.
I am of the view that there should be no provision in this regard, but I realize this would be asking too much because this sort of inducement does take place today. Since it is recognized that it takes place, some sort of restriction should be placed upon it. The amendment I propose to move is not much different from the present wording of paragraph (b); it simply puts a limit of $100 on the expenditure that may be made for such purposes. I am proposing a new subparagraph

(b), in substitution of the present provision, and it reads as follows:

Mr. Chairman, one of the things that I think bothers a number of members is the fact that the Act refers to any individual other than a candidate. That individual might be someone who could afford a $5,000 expenditure for non-alcoholic light refreshments, including ice cream, etc., for a picnic or rally the day before election day. On the surface at least this is an advantage to someone who has a wealthy supporter or contributor. This really is somewhat of a perversion of the democratic process. If that kind of expenditure is desired, why should it not go through the hands of the official agent and be reported as an election expense on the documents which must be filed? It seems to me this kind of expenditure is not accountable in any way under this section. That is the reason we want the $100 limit. It would not, of course, apply to small meetings. No one is going to run around counting the cookies and cups of coffee which are served to see whether the $100 limit is exceeded.
The intent of this section is to allow within reason those expenditures by an individual for refreshments of this kind at a meeting or gathering. Surely it is not unreasonable to place a limit on the amount. No one is going to worry about it unless the amount is blatantly in excess of $100. Then someone could take the matter up under the Elections Act and lay charges accordingly.
If a candidate or an individual on behalf of a candidate wished to spend $100, $500, $1,000 or $5,000 for this purpose he could very easily do so at a large outdoor function. That money should be given to the candidate's official agent and accounted for as an election expense. The official agent should report it accordingly. It seems to me this is a much better and more proper manner of doing it. That is the real reason this group submits this amendment for the consideration of hon. members.
We are not particularly worried about small meetings and gatherings that hon. members hold in many places in their respective constituencies. We feel we should guard against the abuses that can and undoubtedly will take place in some areas under this type of provision. When this happens it is unfair to
other parties and other candidates. As I said earlier, this is a perversion of the electoral process. The amount is not accounted for and does not appear before the eyes of the public for examination.
We hope the President of the Privy Council and other hon. members will reconsider this matter and will be willing to accept this restriction as a proper one under the Elections Act.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to move what I am sure the committee will be happy to learn is our last amendment to this bill. As has been pointed out many times, during meetings of the Standing Committee, on second reading and in committee of the whole, it is the desire of all hon. members to widen the provisions of this act so that the maximum number of people can attend at the polls and vote. It is our view that this can be achieved by the advance poll, and therefore I move:
Advance polls shall be open between the hours of eight o'clock in the forenoon and eight o'clock in the afternoon of Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Monday, the eleventh, tenth, ninth and seventh days before the ordinary polling day, and shall not be open at any other time.

Canada Elections Act
The purpose of this amendment is to increase the number of days of the advance poll from two to four. It may be argued that little or insufficient use is made of the advance poll to merit increasing it. I think this is because the public have not been well informed on the use of the advance poll; also, previously there were restrictions on who could vote at the advance poll. But it seems to me it is now possible for anyone to cast a ballot at the advance poll, and therefore greater use should be made of it. I am sure the Chief Electoral Officer will now do a much better job of informing the public of their rights in regard to the advance poll and the manner in which it can be used. This should encourage the use of the advance poll and offset any argument about the expense involved.
I appreciate that to increase the advance poll from two days to four days would decrease the time available for the revised lists to come from the revising officers to the deputy returning officer, but if this amendment is accepted I will move two consequential amendments. These are to rules 39 and 58, schedule A, clause 18. They were introduced by the hon. member for Selkirk and allowed to stand. The amendments would move the last day of revision back to the fourteenth day before polling day rather than the thirteenth day, thus allowing three days instead of two for the transmission of the revised lists from the revising officers to the deputy returning officer. I hope hon. members will agree that this amendment will widen the opportunity for people to cast their ballot and I commend it to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to take up much of the time of the committee. I support this amendment. It will improve the opportunity for people to vote at advance polls. I understand the system has been very unsatisfactory in the past. In the case of my own riding, it has served very few people. It is an improvement, however, and I urge the committee to support the motion.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, and not just because it is the hon. member's last amendment, that I also support this amendment. In many parts of the country four days would not be necessary, but because in some parts this amount of time is

necessary, and being desirous of widening the opportunity for people to vote conveniently, I think this is a helpful suggestion.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to draw to the attention of the committee some of the consequences of this amendment, in terms of formal procedure, which have been brought to my attention. The principal concern about our having advance polls on four days instead of two is that it would increase the risk of tampering with ballot boxes. The ballot box is made available and set up on the first day of the advance poll and under our present system the poll only has to be reopened once. With this amendment the poll would be reopened two additional times and it would be around for that additional period. In the view of the Chief Electoral Officer, this increases the risk of the ballot box being tampered with.
The cost would be exactly double, but perhaps that is not the most important consideration. One of the most important changes in the section is one which the committee recommended to subclause 3 of clause 92. Under the present provisions of the act, notice of the advance poll is published only on the twelfth day before the ordinary polling day which is only two clear days before the first day of the advance poll.
It is proposed by this amendment that the notice will be published on the thirtieth day before polling day, so that much longer notice will be available. This is perhaps the most significant amendment to the advance poll proposal. One consequential amendment to which the hon. member referred would create a further problem with regard to transmitting the revised list of electors to the advance poll. The notice of objection to the entry of an elector on the revised list, which must be mailed on Friday, would certainly not be received until Monday and therefore would be virtually useless. In other words, the possibility of objection proceedings under the revisions system would be effectively reduced by this change. I hope the committee will consider these procedural and administrative problems which could arise if the amendment were adopted.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This amendment will, of course, if adopted, have the effect of returning the Elections Act to the state in which it was before the last election campaign as far as this particular area is concerned.
Canada Elections Act
Hon. members will recall that the Broadcasting Act was amended some years ago, reducing the blackout period or moratorium on broadcasting in political campaigns to the day before election day, plus election day itself. The Elections Act as it stood at that time had a broadcasting blackout which was operative for two days before polling day. During the last election campaign there was some doubt on the part of all parties about which provision was most binding. Some acted on the assumption that the Elections Act was applicable because it was the specific law which applied, while others acted on the basis that the Broadcasting Act was applicable because it had been most recently passed in time.
To a degree, then, this controversy will be resolved by reason of the fact that the Elections Act will now be the most recent. For my part, I would be inclined to agree with the decision of Parliament in the sixties. I do not really follow the merit of the two-day moratorium and I would be glad to hear argument on this point. I believe the committee did not deal with the question at great length.

Mr. Chairman, My recollection is that the reduction from two days to one is a proposal by the government which differs from the recommendation of the committee. I presume the committee members here are convinced, as I am, that the original proposition did have merit. This provision has proven in many cases to be a valuable and-I believe the electorate would say-a valued reprieve from heavy electioneering. Whether the people who own the networks would prefer a 24-hour period to a 48-hour period is immaterial to me as one who has been involved in wondering how in heaven's name the bills for television and radio were ever to be paid in any case.
[DOT] (8:10p.m.)
Considering that the election campaign period has not been diminished by the introduction of a permanent voters' list, our people are subjected to a campaign lasting something like eight weeks, during which time the bombardment through the media becomes quite intense. I think there is great value in having what one might call an intellectual cooling off period. I have talked this question over with many of my colleagues in various parties and we have found the 48 hours to be very valuable to constituents as well as extremely useful to the organizations as a means of taking

June 25, 1970
Canada Elections Act
one's breath, as it were, on the Friday night, with a full day Saturday and then the sabbath. By Monday people have mulled over all the issues and the time has come for personal contact. I have also checked with people in provincial election campaigns where there is no specific blackout under the Broadcasting Act, and they expressed a pretty strong feeling that they wished to heaven the period of blackout had been 48 hours rather than 24 hours. On the aspect of expense alone, this matter is extremely important and it does clear the air of argument.
The committee may recall that it was originally thought there was value in the blackout in preventing any last minute feedback with no opportunity to straighten out any distortion or to challenge an outrageous allegation. There is still value in this. I have the feeling that after the poor public have been hammered at for eight weeks, a 48-hour respite before they go to the polls is not too much to ask. If I might discuss another piece of legislation, I think the logical step at some time is to make the Broadcasting Act consistent with the Canada Elections Act. I have never heard of any member of the public being so thirsty for an extra political speech that he had requested an extra day. I hear the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce suggesting something over there.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He said, "You don't know the people in Drummondville".

Some places offer purer springs and perhaps thereby inculcate a heavier thirst, but I think God was always able to convince my intelligent people, within the last 48 hours, what course of action they should take. But seriously, to avoid last minute contradictions, last minute pollsters, last minute repetition of Gallup polls, last minute influencing and particularly last minute bombardment of the public, I think the 48-hour blackout, which has worked very well, should be restored.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he like to see all forms of advertising in broadcasting, such as broadcasting by loudspeaker, eliminated; or is he thinking of a two-day moratorium for radio and TV only?

I do not want to sound like a geront on this matter, but in 1960 there was some discussion of this question. In fact, an amendment was made and many members of the committee, those from the province of

Quebec in particular, pointed out that prohibiting broadcasting by loudspeaker even on the Sunday was very unhelpful because the pattern in the province of Quebec when there were gatherings on the Sunday before election day was to use a loudspeaker, which was thought very helpful. I remember the hon. member for Carleton saying that he was quite in favour of that but it would not do him any good to have a Sunday meeting in his constituency. I remember we removed that provision from the act. However, at the moment I am thinking only of radio and television. I know of no way of giving the newspaper publisher a slack day; all I had in mind was the radio and television media.

Mr. Chairman, I would put a question to the President of the Privy Council. I do not understand why there is this kind of restriction on radio and television but no restriction on the use of loudspeakers or on newspapers. What is the reason for that?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the point is well taken. I suppose there is a feeling that newspapers do not have the same immediacy and impact as the broadcasting media. There is a restriction on loudspeakers operating on polling day. I suppose it is a question of the immediacy of its effect. The assumption I was making was that newspaper advertising, particularly on election day, has less impact than radio and television. Loudspeakers would probably not be used on the Sunday for reasons of good taste.

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of factors involved in this question. Many people take the view that because there has been a containment within the Elections Act, broadcasting by radio and television has not been permitted up until now during the 48 hours preceding polling day. This has carried with it in the minds of many people the implication that no campaigning should be conducted during the same period. I am sure every member of the House has heard someone say that he thought the campaigning ended on the Friday night, either at eight o'clock in the evening or at midnight, and that there was this period of the Saturday and Sunday, with an election being held on a Monday, as is usually the case, for quiet contemplation of the issues. The companion feeling was also expressed that the people wish this to be so in order that they have a respite from the inundation of radio and television propaganda, news propaganda and last minute efforts to convince people to vote for one party or another.
June 25, 1970

Perhaps this has been brought into sharp focus by the introduction of television into the communications media which is, in effect, a sort of invasion of a person's home and privacy-though he can, of course, repel that invasion by simply switching off the set. It has also been brought into sharp focus by the activation of political party propaganda mechanisms to the point where they will have maximum effect. The conclusion has been drawn that the maximum effect will be felt nearer to election day rather than further from it, though the general public has reacted against this. As I assess the situation from what people have said, they appreciate and enjoy the 48-hour prohibition. This prohibition is that during the last two days of an election campaign privacy shall not be invaded by political propagandizing on radio, television and the like.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
There are elements within the newsmedia that do not do this. Some elements have up to now interpreted the prohibition in the Elections Act in respect of radio and television broadcasting to apply to news generally and have refused to distribute election information during that 48-hour period. They recognize the fact that the general public at that stage has had enough of inundation, advertising, promolion, propagandizing and exhortation by way of radio and television. They want a period of tranquility and non-invasion of their thoughts; they want a period when there is no political pushing and promoting.
Many people have probably made up their minds by this time. I think if you were to draw a graph of the situation you would find that as you get closer to polling day fewer and fewer people remain undecided. Perhaps the majority would say they had come to a decision and determined how they would vote. For this reason they do not need to be exhorted any longer, they do not need to be told any longer about the values of this party or the weaknesses of that party, they no longer need to be told the virtues of this candidate as opposed to another candidate, because they have decided. The people who have not decided are fewer and fewer as you get closer to election day. I think we must give cognizance to this fact.
The President of the Privy Council has said there is a proscription within the act and on election day one shall not use loud-hailers, loudspeakers or travelling microphone-amplifier systems to exhort people to vote a 22478-53
Canada Elections Act
certain way or not to vote a certain way. The admission is that even on the day of polling there should be quietude without propagandizing through the news media. The government has also admitted that on the day prior to polling day there should be a broadcasting quietude; that is a day when there should be no radio or television promotional activity. It is hard to draw a line as to how long this period should be. One might suggest two days, three days, four days or 56 hours. Whichever one you pick is an arbitrary period, admittedly, but the fact is that for many years we have had in the Elections Act the concept that there should be a two-day period, usually a Saturday and a Sunday.
Most elections fall on Monday. I think the last election was deliberately designed to take advantage of St. Jean Baptiste Day. It was held on a Tuesday. That was a political decision. As far back as I can remember, and for many years before that, elections have been held on Monday, with the concept that the Saturday and Sunday should be days of tranquility, with relief from political pressure, propaganda, advertising, pushing and promoting. The general public appreciates the tranquility and enjoys this period. During the last week and a half or the last two weeks, depending on the judgment of the candidate and the party, there is a concentration of pressure. This two-day period of Saturday and Sunday should be a time of relative sanctity without one being subjected to the intensity of political campaign pressures. It should be a period of quietude and reflection for the voters. I endorse the idea of retaining this provision which has been in our Elections Act for many years.
Apropos the question asked earlier as to whether this proscription should apply just to radio and television-we are dealing with a particular section of the act that directs itself only to radio, television advertising and promotion-I endorse the idea that newspaper advertising and all other forms of political campaigning should cease on these days. I realize at the moment of saying or even thinking about it that it is hard to define what is political campaigning. Election day itself involves political campaigning. The fact that a candidate is present at a polling station, smiling and saying hello to the people, is political campaigning. Unless you remove the candidate and all his campaign workers you cannot have anything but campaigning right up to the last ballot being cast. There is cam-

June 25, 1970
Canada Elections Act
paigning even after the polls are closed, by candidates who go around to thank the deputy returning officer. These candidates are looking to the future.
There should be some sort of legalistic or legislative cut-off date after which inundation by propaganda and information is prohibited as much as possible. Much of the information is false. I do not use that word in its true sense, because political campaigning is designed to advance the cause of one party or one candidate over another. There should be such a period of rest. I think the Saturday and Sunday before the election on Monday, the normal polling day under the Elections Act, is a sufficient period. We must also remember the view expressed by the Standing Committee. It had a majority of Liberal members. The committee studied this and many other questions in depth. That committee did its best to bring about a good Elections Act which was fair, just and equitable. The Committee was made up of Liberals, Conservatives, NDP members and members of the Ral-liement Creditiste, who 1 might say were not in attendance very often. The committee made an attempt to treat this matter in a non-partisan way, without advancing partisan objectives.
The majority of the members of the committee felt that a two-day period was sufficient. The members thought we should be developing electoral law and should not succumb to the view expressed about the provisions of the Radio Act in relation to the Monday or a 24-hour period.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question?

My friend may not ask a question at this juncture. When I have concluded my remarks I will entertain questions and do my best to answer them. The fundamental point is the one I made at the outset. The general public appreciate this period of quietude, tranquility and noninvolvement, without pressure through propaganda on radio and television. This fact should have the greatest impact on us. I think we should pay attention to the desires of the electorate in this regard. So far as I have been able to assess the situation, their desire is that all campaigning should end on the Friday night. Most people have made up their minds by the Friday night preceding an election and they should have this period of noninvolvement, tranquility and quietude. They

want this period in order to reflect and make a determination about how they should vote on election day.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I listened with some interest to the remarks of the hon. member. I agree with his observation that the committee, in looking at this matter, was not guided by partisan considerations. I believe, however, that the consensus of the committee is in the report which is before us. After considerable discussion on the point, the majority view was that the period should be one day.
Where does this appear in the report?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant
speechtext:
I attended the committee meeting at that time. I was not consistently a member. I recall the vote being put during the proceedings that day. I could find the reference, but I do not think my memory is wrong in this regard. I think the majority opinion was that it should be a period of one day before election day. Members of the committee recognized the fact as expressed by the hon. member for Skeena, that our federal elections are held on a Monday and will continue to be so held in the future. I do not believe there is any indication to the contrary. The prohibition against campaigning on Sunday is not contained entirely within the Canada Elections Act; it is also contained in municipal ordinances. In addition, many voters take exception to any political activity on Sunday. The problem is that usually there are a large number of activities on the Saturday before the Monday election.
The committee was anxious to be uniform and not discriminate among the news media. The newspapers were perfectly free to print everything they wanted to print on the Saturday before the Monday election. Door-to-door canvassers also were perfectly free to invade what the hon. member called the sanctity of the voters, including a number of supporters of this party. In this regard there was a considerable amount of confusion and discrimination among the news media. It was felt that if we were to apply the 48-hour rule consistently, across the board, we would have to apply it to newspapers and that in respect of the Broadcasting Act we would have to upset long-established practices which have been built into our electoral system since the beginning of this country. This was a decision of the majority of the committee after consid-
June 25, 1970

Canada Elections Act
erable debate and after listening to many arguments. It was advocated that there was only one way in which to be consistent, and that was to put the one-day rule into effect and rigidly enforce it.
The idea is that there will be no campaigning on the Sunday before election day, no advertising and no door-to-door canvassing or use of sound equipment. This rule in no small part would be enforced, as would any general rule, by the standards of good taste in the community and a desire not to offend the electors, as much as by the prohibition which would be written into the act. No matter what members think, the fact is that if the two-day rule were put into the act, this would not stop most of the activities described as reprehensible, and there would be some discrimination between the press and other activities. On balance, members of the committee thought that the one-day rule would be enforceable and would be consistent with the good taste of the community. Any other rule, in the opinion of the committee, would not be enforceable.

Mr. Chairman, I have a small reaction to the remarks of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. I do not think this provision refers to the use of loudspeakers at public meetings. To that extent there is no effort made to curtail what in fact is the amplification of the human voice at a political meeting. Also, it should be borne in mind that there are communities in Canada which have Sunday newspapers. Even the 24-hour blackout will not cure this problem. I am very sorry this question has caused division in an otherwise harmonious day, but as I understand it there has been the thought in this one area at least that we could cut down some of the raucous, cacophonous sounds which are part of a healthy political campaign. Of course, this in itself would not stop the hon. member for Skeena travelling about his constituency on the Saturday. He might even do so on Sunday, though I as a God-fearing Presbyterian go to church on Sunday and hope for the best.
Not all day.

Not all day, but after being involved in politics so long, I need it. One has to be pragmatic about this matter. It cannot be suggested that by moving from 48 hours to 24 hours we are bringing in a foolproof measure, and that with the 24-hour period we will have a total blackout for 24 22478-534
hours whereas with the 48-hour period we had only a partial blackout. I say again that the 48-hour period would work. If this means amending the Broadcasting Act, I agree with the hon. member for Skeena that it should be amended. It is no more difficult to amend the Broadcasting Act than it is to amend the Canada Elections Act. I have studied this question very carefully and I see no reason why this avenue should be left open any nearer to the actual day of decision. I should like to think that the Canadian people make up their minds after reflection and consideration. I think they are helped, as the hon. member for Skeena said, by having their living-rooms and lawns to themselves, in so far as the electronic media are concerned for that weekend, the Saturday and Sunday. There are many fine Canadians to whom Saturday is in fact the Sabbath day.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Skeena said there are many people who would like to have a 48-hour prohibition against television and radio. I suppose there are a great many people who would like to have an eight-week prohibition against television and radio in an election campaign. But I am wondering about the sanctity of this one day. The gentleman from Skeena said that the day before the election, the Sunday, should be sacred, quiet and peaceful. He suggested that it should not be interrupted by dirty politics. I think this is the root of the whole question. There would seem to be the connotation that political activity on television or radio has some semblance of dirty business.
At one time, possibly, politics was dirty business and if one were a Presbyterian like the hon. gentleman for Hillsborough, one would wish to avoid politics at all costs, especially on Sunday. Now we have this clamour for a 48-hour prohibition so that the Sunday would be peaceful, especially on television, and so the people would not be interrupted by politics and would be able to enjoy the hockey games, "I Love Lucy," Ed Sullivan, the "FBI" and all the other programs which are shown on television on Sunday. The reason is that politics is just too horrible a subject to contemplate on a Sunday. Now they want to include Saturday.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
No.

You want not only Sunday prohibited but also Saturday. Under this provi-

June 25, 1970
Canada Elections Act
sion there would be a 24-hour prohibition, not a 48-hour prohibition. I suggest that a large number of people who are quite busy during the week, especially the week before an election, would have no objection to sitting at home on Saturday, if that is the day they want to sit at home, listening to the arguments put forth by all sides. Maybe on that day they would make up their minds. If they do not want to listen to the program, they can easily go out or switch to another channel; not every channel is carrying the election. I think the argument makes no sense. I think the 24-hour prohibition under the act is enough.
People do not contemplate politics on a Sunday, believe me. They contemplate many other things, the least of which is politics. If they had made up their minds on the previous Saturday, it would make no difference. If they had not made up their minds, possibly the Saturday within the 48-hour period would give them the opportunity to do so and would be of great benefit to them and to the country.

Mr. Chairman, I support the amendment which would in effect reinstate the provisions of the present Elections Act regarding the 48 hours prohibition rather than changing it, as proposed, to 24 hours. I do so because I rely on my memory as well as does the hon. member for Ottawa West. As I recall-I stand to be corrected on this-the committee was badly divided and it may well have erred, because there is nothing in the report concerning this item. I have gone over the report hurriedly and I may have missed it, but as far as I can see there is nothing in it on this item.
As I recall, the committee was badly divided on this question. By a slight majority it agreed that we would revert to the 24-hour prohibition. The lack of unanimity crossed party lines. The House has already set up a special committee on election expenses. I suggest this is another item-arguments were presented along this line earlier today-that might well be left until we have a report with recommendations from the committee on election expenses. The present act contains a provision for 48 hours. I think we should leave it that way until we have the proposed legislation.
I am not of the same opinion as my friends the hon. member for Hillsborough and the hon. member for Skeena regarding time for quietude and time to meditate on how I am going to vote on the Monday. I suspect that I,

like most voters will head for the lake that day and I am not likely to think about how I shall vote on election day. I would rather put it on more hardnosed, realistic grounds.
This provision will give aid and comfort to the broadcasters, who will get another 24 hours of selling broadcasting time to political parties and candidates who might be suckers enough to blow some more money, because in fact most of them will have run out of money by that time, in a last-gasp, panic effort to stay elected or become elected. I also put forward a similar argument to the one I presented earlier today, that this provision would give an unfair advantage to a party or candidate who happens to have some money or supporters who can throw in a few hundred or a few thousand dollars for a last minute broadcast. The last effort to grab the voter demeans and perverts the electoral process. I understand that the Broadcasting Act provides for one day, while the Elections Act provides for two days. It seems to me that the Elections Act should take priority over the Broadcasting Act. Therefore, the Broadcasting Act should be amended, not the Elections Act, particularly until the recommendations and report of the committee on election expenses have been made.
Like the hon. member for Ottawa West, I am only relying on my memory but, as I recall, the committee agreed that in this regard the Broadcasting Act should be amended rather than the Elections Act. Either one, or both of us could be wrong on this point. That is why I think the committee of the whole should accept the amendment of the hon. member for Hillsborough until we receive the report of the committee on election expenses and the proposed legislation. I see no reason why this committee should give aid and comfort to the broadcasting industry, which will only add another 10 per cent to its tariffs because it happened to be an election period. I think we should do everything we can to head off and limit the last minute, panic, exorbitant expenditures by candidates of parties, no matter who they may be. I hope we will adopt the amendment of the hon. member for Hillsborough and leave the act as it is. We can go into the matter in greater detail at the next session of Parliament. I hope the committee will support this amendment.

I know it is not the usual procedure to harp back to the proceedings of the Standing Committee, but I take exception to what the hon. member from across the way

suggested when he said that the Standing Committee supported the one-day blackout. In my firm recollection, endorsed by what my colleague the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East has shown me, it was the other way round.

Mr. Chairman, that is obvious. When one takes direction, as the hon. gentleman did, one does not have to grasp anything.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to move an amendment to clause 99, subclause 1,
Canada Elections Act
in order to clarify a point that is rather vague. In respect of the definition of "broadcasting" in the fourth line on page 191, clause 99, subclause 1, after the word "broadcasts" I should like to insert the words "via radio, television, or loudspeaker". Most of us have agreed that there should be a period of peace and quiet in which people can decide how to cast their ballot. Although I think one day is sufficient, other hon. members may think there should be two days. In any event, if we allow messages to be blasted into the homes of unwilling listeners, this is not ensuring peace and quiet. If there is an argument for a moratorium on radio and television, surely there is a greater argument with respect to the use of loudspeakers. At least radio and television can be turned off, but this is not possible in respect of broadcasting from a car the day before the election. I suggest that this amendment should be adopted.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the hon. gentleman a question. In his interpretation, does loudspeaker include a loudspeaker at a private meeting? A microphone is a loudspeaker. How did the hon. member define loudspeaker; must it be a loudspeaker attached to a moving vehicle?
You are a loud speaker yourself.

Mr. Chairman, there are many definitions of loud speaker; many people have accused me of being one without my having any electronic aid. Would the President of the Privy Council care to suggest in which clause such an amendment would be appropriate?

Mr. Chairman, I am amazed that a government backbencher asks the advice of the government front bench on a matter that is not government policy. The
