matter I wish to raise is of more serious consequence, that is, the matter of prohibition.

speechtext:
We
abolished that this afternoon.

Apart from the fact that everybody but the hon. member for Ontario knows that television is included in the area of broadcasting, surely we must consider this question in terms of campaigning. Maybe this is what we are getting at, a period in which to reflect. I think the member for York East put the matter in perspective when he asked what kind of loudspeaker was meant, and was it one that runs up and down the street. That point was not clarified. Is it one in use at a public meeting? This type is permissible.
This raises the question of ordinary canvassing when someone comes knocking at the door early in the morning. Are we going to proscribe this? Is it less an invasion of privacy than the loud-hailer travelling up and down the street? Which is more offensive? Telephone calls soliciting votes are also more offensive than the loud-hailer on the street, in my opinion. At least the loud-hailer passes by and sometimes is gone before one hears the message.
I think this point puts in perspective the question of having a period of quietude. To say that broadcasting should be prohibited takes the question beyond radio and television. But the member for Ontario talks about loudspeakers without defining what he means. Does he mean the mobile loudspeaker? His amendment does not clarify that point. We are here to enact law, not to interpret what somebody means. A court will not pay any attention to what the member for Ontario meant but will undoubtedly come to the conclusion that a loudspeaker used in a hall to broadcast outside the hall is the same sort of thing as a loudspeaker which is mobile because it is mounted on a truck. If we are to talk about prohibition we must be inclusive. Consider candidates campaigning in northern climes. If we have an election in the middle of winter, why not ship us off to Florida for three or four months?
Hear, hear!

We might make the prohibition operative for two or three weeks before election day. This is what we are talking about. We are also talking about the

effect of a campaign in an urban area1 as distinct from a rural area. As the member for York East said, one can turn the television switch to a channel being broadcast from somewhere in the United States, or you can hook up to a mechanism which we do not have at home, cablevision.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
The law that we will pass provides that you shall not broadcast from outside the country a political program or political exhortation into the country, and the only news items and the like shall be carried. So it may be all right for the hon. member for York East to make his proposals: he comes from the Toronto area and Toronto is almost a province by itself. It is an enclave and its people have little knowledge of places such as British Columbia. The reverse of the situation is also true. But people in Toronto who are involved in election campaigns have no knowledge of the situation that may exist in rural areas-in Skeena, for example.
Allow me to relate the situation of my neighbour who represents the constituency of Prince George-Peace River. The area is served by one television station which is a CBC affiliate. That is all. You cannot turn to another channel; you turn your set on or off. We know that people like to watch television programs. But most of the people in northern Canada are captive. People in the far reaches of British Columbia are captive to an even greater extent because there the CBC decides not only what to show but shows it in package form. In some parts of the province we see on television hockey games that were played three weeks before. We get late in the evening, afternoon programs that are designed for the housewife. Children's programs, designed to be shown in urban areas in the monring, are shown in parts of British Columbia at supper time or early evening. That shows how captive we are. In these areas there is a reactiion against certain types of political broadcasts and the inundation of political ideas because there is no alternative to them.
Will the hon. member permit a question at this time? I was wondering if the hon. member for-
Skeena.
See, they don't know British Columbia.

-Skeena has considered that the mobile loudspeaker would offend anti-

noise bylaws in every reasonably developed municipality. You might say that a charge could be laid, but by the time the charge is heard in court, one month after the event, the election will be over and the fine probably will be $50. Is it fair that a politician should be able to offend that bylaw and pay a $50 fine? Should we not recognize that such noise constitutes pollution and annoys people? Should we not put into this act, where it can be meaningful, the provision that the election of candidates who break the law in this respect-people with mobile loudspeakers- may be put in jeopardy?

I do not, on principle, disagree with that statement. I suggest to the hon. gentleman that the party he supports knows a lot more about pollution than most others and is doing less about it than anybody else. The greatest offenders in the area of noise pollution are hon. gentlemen opposite. If the question of the hon. gentleman opposite has any validity, I submit that this prohibition is valid two days before an election even more than it is on the day before an election. My hon. friend will not accept that because he has been told by the President of the Privy Council to do as he is told.
That is not true.

It is true.
I tell my hon. friend from Ontario that the proof of this will be found when he votes. The proof is not in what my hon. friend says.

Mr. Chairman, I absolutely
resent the hon. member's suggesting that I have been ordered by the President of the Privy Council or anybody else to vote any way on this or any other issue that I have had to vote on. It is just not true. The hon. member seems to think he can say these nasty things and get away with them. I say that he jolly well cannot.

Mr. Chairman, I could not agree with you more, with great respect. I wish you had taken that tack when the hon. member for Ontario ran away with himself, but you obviously did not want to do that.

Mr. Chairman, I ask
myself, where has the sweet harmony of this afternoon gone? I expected that when the hon. member for Ontario rose he would suggest that we abolish even the 24-hour blackout, since we have heard how virtuous a matter is the exposure of the public to the electronics media. I am somewhat concerned-I hope the hon. member for York Centre will be satisfied with my presentation, because he commented on this matter earlier-by the suggestion that we broaden this prohibition. There is sometimes great wisdom in taking things step by step, rather than making sweeping, all-embracing moves.

In radio and television we knew exactly the type of media we were considering. When you start moving into other areas, you must ask yourself questions. What about the small meeting held by a gentle, mild candidate like myself, with a low voice, so low that even if there were only 40 people in the room he might need a microphone? Might this not be described, perhaps, as an electronic device? One could not use a pre-electronic age megaphone because that would be rather cumbersome.
I still think we are naive in expecting to pass anything in this piece of legislation which will stop people from assembling together on a Saturday; and when they have assembled together it would be rather strange, in this electronics age, if we inhibited the use of those devices which make it easier for one to communicate with those who are about him. So I feel that we are embarking upon an area that is very, very difficult to define. I think we cannot go too far in this area and be productive. I mentioned earlier the question of newspapers and the fact that some publish on Sunday, although I must confess we have only a few. We shall not cover the whole bag here and we must be content with what we have. I regret very much the increasing acerbity of the debate; I trust it will not continue. I have always looked upon the Elections Act not as something designed to give advantage to this side or to that side. I am not reflecting on the vote, but I was a little surprised at the fate of the last amendment. If we look upon this as a piece of legislation which all of us as individuals, irrespective of our political label, are approaching with a desire to make as good as we can, we will make a good deal more progress.

Mr. Chairman, at the outset I intended to second some of the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena. However, the debate became so provocative that I will try to imitate our philosopher from Prince Edward Island; I will try to be very quiet in my presentation to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, unfortunately I cannot support the amendment of the member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) for reasons that seem obvious. In view of my experience in my own province, I feel that several candidates, in rural ridings, on the very last night before the elections, and at times in the morning, when mass comes out, have to convene people

from five or six neighbouring municipalities to give them a last message. There is no other way of reaching them.
The citizens in rural areas are pleased to be invited because it often happens that they are free on Saturday afternoon, or Sunday afternoon or Sunday evening and they enjoy attending local or regional political meetings to hear the arguments of the candidates. In any event, almost all the candidates in the province of Quebec hold similar meetings.
In Quebec, in almost all rural areas and even in small cities such as mine, there is an old custom whereby the night before elections a last meeting is held where loudspeakers are used because in most cases there are more people outside the hall than inside.
As for me, I am very sorry I cannot support the amendment of the member for Ontario.
On the other hand, I should like to move another amendment, because I feel the member for Ontario is totally inconsistent if he intends to forbid propaganda over the radio and television, on the eve of election day and, on that day, when it is allowed in the newspapers.
I cannot admit that a well-to-do candidate could buy a whole page of advertisement in the Sunday newspapers or in papers published on election day while another of lesser means could not do so. It is unfair for all candidates and in my opinion, clause 99 which prohibits publicity the day before or on election day is inconsistent.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to move an amendment. I apologize for having scribbled it down in such haste. I thought other hon. members would have moved it. I therefore move the following words be added in clause 99, after the words "any entertainment or advertising program":
[DOT]-or publishes, distributes or causes to be distributed an advertisement in the newspapers, or circulates printed during that same period-*
In my opinion, it would be only fair to standardize advertising in this respect.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to repeat the explanations I gave earlier but I would still like to see my amendment accepted if it is in order. If it is not, I will gladly abide by your ruling bceause, as I say again, it is totally illogical to allow election advertising in the newspapers while it is blacked out on radio and television the day before the election and on polling day. As I have said, this is a case of serious discrimination towards less well-off candidates which makes it possible to come out at the last moment with a so-called scandal which can affect the results of the election.

Mr. Chairman, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Mongrain) pleases me. Along with my colleagues who are in agreement with me, I wish to assure him that this is really a valid amendment which certainly deserves careful consideration.
I would certainly blame myself, as a representative of a splinter party in the House with a near total lack of financial means, if I did not say publicly how happy and in agreement we are with this amendment.
Since 1962, in every election because adequate financial means are not available to us and especially because we' are fighting financial interests, we suffer from the advertising in some newspapers paid out of well-filled electoral funds. In fact, attacks are made against people or programs taking exception to this system but we have no financial means
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
available to answer them. Since these attacks are launched at the last moment as was said by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, it is physically impossible for us, even with adequate financial means available, to reply.
Mr. Chairman, I believe this amendment is important and I urge my colleagues to give it their support.
During the last provincial election campaign, a striking thing happened in the constituency of Arthabasca. The campaign had been an honest one on all sides up to then- and I give this example to give my colleagues something to think about-except that at the last minute, on the eve of election day, a newspaperman wrote, in collusion with a certain political party, an article that was used as an editorial by a newspaper, and the political party concerned had copies made of that article and distributed them from door to door as well as in automobiles. Mr. Chairman, I would not say such a practice was fraudulent as it was in accordance with the law, but I do not think it was fair play.
I also believe that if we agree on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres, it will show not only that we respect minorities in Canada, but that we provide equal opportunities to everybody, especially to those who do not have sufficient financial means.

I am not sure that I understood the purport of the amendment correctly; I do not have a copy before me. But if my understanding is correct, the effect would be to prohibit advertising in newspapers on the Sunday preceding an election and the distribution by hand or any other means of election material. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say something about the preamble. Since this bill relates to the democratic process, to elections and to the opportunity and the right of people to decide who shall make the laws governing them, I think we ought to change the preamble. It begins with the words "Her Majesty", which some may argue about. It seems common at the moment to object to them. I will not go into that matter at the moment. At any rate, the preamble says:
Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
Canada Elections Act
I think that we should in this law completely eliminate any mention of the Senate, because it has no business here whatsoever.
Hear, hear.

We should certainly not give any consideration to a body that has no responsibility in a political or democratic sense for the people over which it has political authority, and it should have no say whatever in the electoral laws of the nation.

-who, as the hon. member for Skeena has said, with his encyclopaedic knowledge of both the act and electoral processes has been of much assistance to this committee, the standing committee and myself in particular, with my responsibilities for the bill.
I pay particular tribute to the draftsman of the bill, Miss Edythe MacDonald, for preparing this very extensive and complicated bill. With unfailing courtesy she provided amendments to members on both sides of the House, often drafting them at great speed and under considerable pressure. I draw to the attention of the committee that at the same time Miss MacDonald has responsibility for a second bill before us this session, which if anything is more complicated and nearly as voluminous. I express my appreciation to the chairman and the members of the standing committee for their work. I pay special tribute to my Parliamentary Secretary, the member for Missisquoi, who has been of great assistance to me. I also wish to pay tribute to others who have been of great assistance to me in preparing the position for the bill, our former colleague Professor John B. Stewart of St. Francis Xavier University and my present legislative counsel, Mr. Yvon Marcoux. To all of these and the members of this committee, particularly those who were present this afternoon rather than necessarily those present this evening, I express my appreciation in putting through a difficult bill.

Mr. Chairman, I know it is not necessary for me to fill in time because I am sure that Your Honour has found that which he was seeking. In this instance, I would like to add my voice and sentiments to those put forward by the President of the

Privy Council. He is one member of the House with whom I do not find myself consistently in agreement. In this instance, I echo his sentiments.
I have the highest regard for the Chief Electoral Officer with respect to legislation and even more so with respect to the administration of his most important office. I am glad to make the acquaintance of Miss MacDonald. While I do not look forward to reviewing this act soon, I hope it will not be too long before we have her with us again.
Hear, hear!

There is a great deal of work involved in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. Under the old rules it stood in the premier position among the standing committees. Now, committees are listed alphabetically, a practice with which I do not agree. We used to be the premier committee of the House. It is an onerous task to study the Canada Elections Act. I have done it on two occasions. I think much has been accomplished. While the result falls short of the objectives some of us cherish, we are confident that much lias been achieved. Before I take my seat, I wish to observe with reference to the Senate that it just happens in this country we have a bicameral Parliament. That seems to be about it.

On behalf of my party, I wish to echo some of the words of the hon. member for Hillsborough and to add a few. In addition to our thanks to the Chief Electoral Officer and to the charming lady who aided members on both sides of the House with amendments, as well as improving the look of the Chamber a great deal, I want to express our thanks to the President of the Privy Council. I never thought I would live long enough to say that, in light of what occurred a year ago.
We in this party are extremely pleased with the degree of participation, discussion and co-operation. We appreciate the patience and tolerance exhibited by the President of the Privy Council towards the amendments that have been moved and accepted. I may catch hell for this tomorrow, but I sincerely say that in the last number of days on this bill we have had an exercise in the democratic process. It has been an education for all of us in this Chamber and, I hope, an education
June 25, 1970

for people outside the Chamber. I hope we can do this more often on other major pieces of legislation that affect all Canadians in so many ways.

Mr. Chairman, on behalf of my party, I should like to mention our satisfaction with respect to the work done by the committee on privileges and elections and by the committee of the whole, which reviewed the Elections Act in order to improve it.
We cannot miss this opportunity to express also our regards for the Chief Electoral Officer and his staff. That man is not only at the service of the hon. members, but also of the whole population. He is responsible for the Elections Act being at the service of the people. I wish to thank him for that and to assure him of our support and co-operation.
I would also like to extend my regards to Miss MacDonald and to thank her for her excellent work.

Mr. Speaker, may I be allowed a few moments on third reading to say that in addition to the congratulatory words expressed earlier in committee of the whole there is, I am sure, a feeling shared by many members in all corners of the House that more must be done than has been done in this chamber and will be done by the printing of a new act. Some effort must be made to acquaint the Canadian public with what is new in the electoral law, a law which we have revised in a major manner.
I should like to make a plea to the government and to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) in particular to see that the budget of the Chief Electoral Officer is doubled or trebled if necessary to enable him to acquaint the Canadian public with their wider rights and privileges under this law, rights which will enable them to exercise their franchise in what I believe to be a new and better manner than ever before in the history of this country. I believe expenditures for this purpose ought not to be criticized by any party or by those who write columns in the news media. In fact, I hope that the office of the Chief Electoral Officer will be encouraged in this work by editorials and by articles of a voluminous nature immediately before and during the next election campaign.

June 25, 1970
Canada Elections Act
The new law is not all new, but unless this kind of exercise is carried out there is likely to be a great deal of confusion and possibly, after the election, ill will which will harm the effect of what I believe to be some worthwhile improvements to the act. It is incumbent upon government and Parliament to provide the Chief Electoral Officer with the funds and facilities to enable him to do this job.
On behalf of the New Democratic Party I should like to say that we believe we have made a major error in neglecting to provide some method of absentee polling, no matter how restricted. As soon as it became apparent that because of the relatively small size of our population and its scattered distribution we could not draw up a permanent electoral list, there was a tendency on the part of too many members both in the committee and in this House to throw out all possibility of an absentee ballot. The experience of a number of provinces whose populations are thin and widely scattered shows that an absentee balloting system could be made to work in the absence of a permanent voters' list. I still feel we could have provided an absentee polling system for at least certain groups in certain circumstances. This would have obviated the necessity for many of the other provisions we have been obliged to include in order to widen the opportunity for people to cast their ballots.
In other words, when we eliminated the prospect of a permanent list we threw out the baby with the bath water. I believe we could have introduced some form of absentee ballot, albeit limited. I hope that in another session of this Parliament, perhaps following the report of the committee on election expenses, we can amend this law even further to provide a method of absentee balloting. This will enable us to do away with many of the other facilities we have tried to incorporate in the bill. In any case, I do not believe they will prove to be all that workable. I specifically mention the system of proxy voting and repeat what I said on second reading. I hope I am wrong, but I predict that it will prove to be cumbersome from an administrative point of view and extremely inconvenient for voters. We may still have to go through this experience for one election in order to learn the lesson, but I hope that we shall decide to re-examine this bill next session and provide a system of absentee balloting.

I close by thanking members of my own party and all other members who sat on the Standing Committee and took part in what I think have been several wonderful days in committee of the whole in arriving at this legislation. I believe it to have been one of the better exercises carried out by this House and regret very much that it should have received so little attention and publicity outside this chamber.

Mr. Speaker, I shall moralize but briefly at this stage of the important measure before us. We tend to harp upon our own particular string. I have not yet been convinced that we were wise in not making provision for a permanent voters' list. Even that vast nation, the subcontinent of India, is now in process of compiling a permanent roll. I agree this has been a most excellent debate. However, I believe it is fundamental that efforts be made to publicize the important changes we have introduced into our electoral machinery. As I said this afternoon, I much regret the inadequate attention which has been given to this important debate by the press gallery and by the media. In the six Parliaments in which I have served so far, never have I seen a measure so important receive such inadequate and inferior treatment.
Shame!

This makes it all the more important that the suggestion of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) should be carried out. I think, too, that the weight of the work we have borne demonstrates the importance of frequent review of our electoral machinery. We should not allow years and years to pass and then have a ponderous exercise in redrafting. It is extremely important, I think, that we keep our electoral machinery well tuned and sharply honed to the needs of a vibrant, healthy majority.
[DOT] (10:50 p.m.)
Having said that, I think we have done well here. Perhaps this debate was neglected by the media because it was so lacking in partisan sharpness and so much given to something a little above partisan cut and thrust. But I have no sorrow on that score at all because I think we have acquitted ourselves well. I think this piece of electoral legislation is a vast improvement, though not quite so
June 25, 1970

good as legislation I would have evolved had I full scope to do so. However, as I say, it is a great improvement and I trust it will serve Canada well.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to join others at this stage in adding one or two brief comments. First of all, may I express to the members of the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections and the members of the House my personal appreciation of the thoughtful consideration they have given to taking the first meaningful step forward in many years to further the protection of the secrecy of the franchise of the Canadian forces voters. What we have done should indicate to this particular group that we are indeed concerned about them, that we did address ourselves to the question of absentee voting and to other methods by which the secrecy of the franchise might have been assured in even greater measure. Regrettably, and perhaps for a variety of sound reasons, at this particular time we were not able to go to the extent we might have gone in this regard. However, we have made meaningful progress.
The two previous speakers addressed themselves to the importance to the Canadian people of the measure we are now concluding. Like the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie), I too hope it will not be ten years before we return to the bill. As he and others particularly the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) pointed out, there are still deficiencies in the manner in which Canadians are given an opportunity to exercise their franchise. Similarly, there are glaring deficiences with regard to the elderly and those who by virtue of their occupation are net able to qualify for or to be present at the advance poll or on the day of voting, or to avail themselves of the proxy vote.
I must differ with my friend from Regina-Lake Centre in his pessimism about the practical appreciation of the proxy vote. Another great province, the province where all great political wisdom was born well over 200 years ago, has implemented this provision and it has worked. There has not been the abuse of the system that some hon. members have feared, perhaps with justification as a result of their own experience. The proxy in our province has not been abused to any widespread extent. Indeed, it has afforded to thou-
Canada Elections Act
sands of Nova Scotians who otherwise would not have been able to do so for reasons of physical incapacity or of employment, the opportunity to exercise their franchise.
I also think the extension of the right to vote to Canadians of 18 years and over is another meaningful step. As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre said, it is important that this and all the other very meaningful aspects of the changes that have been made, both in committee of the whole House and in the Standing Committee, be communicated to all Canadians. The method of doing so has been discussed in the Standing Committee. If there was no direction given there, there was at least clear evidence relating to the wishes of the committee and in this respect there was some degree of unanimity.
If it is not too late, I should like to join previous speakers in expressing my own appreciation to the Chief Electoral Officer and his staff for the tremendous assistance they have given us, and also to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) for the manner in which he conducted the deliberations of the Standing Committee when it had this measure before it. I think it is a measure of the wisdom and maturity of this House that the bill was dealt with on a non-partisan basis. Unlike some comments made earlier this evening, perhaps partly in jest, I did not suspect more than once or twice that the President of the Privy Council was trying to lead anybody. On the contrary, I think he did an excellent job and should be commended for it.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member for Dart-mouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) telling us about how much the province of Nova Scotia is the fount of all wisdom, dating back some 200 years, and how we the Parliament of Canada have now adopted this very wise provision relating to proxy voting that his province has put into effect, may I be permitted to point out, because I know the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) would be too timorous and humble to do so, that the province of Nova Scotia undoubtedly adopted the proxy system from Ontario, where it has been in effect since some years prior to its introduction in Nova Scotia.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

FISHERIES-MANITOBA GOVERNMENT OFFER OF FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ESTABLISH PROCESSING PLANT IN SELKIRK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday of this week I asked the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) whether he had yet received an offer from the government of Manitoba of additional incentives to encourage the continued location of the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation processing plant in Selkirk. At that time the minister indicated that he had not yet received an offer. I assume he now has the offer and that he will be able to give at least a preliminary opinion on it.
[DOT] (11:00 p.m.)
In our last encounter on this subject I am afraid that both the minister and myself were guilty of casting more heat than light on the subject of the optimum location. I in no way wish to suggest, in saying this, that I was wrong in asserting that the matter of location of the plant, because of the possible conflict of interest between the 6,000 fishermen whose incomes are being attended to by the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation and the needs of some 20,000 people living in the interlake and coming under an ARDA-FRED [Mr. Howard (Skeena).l
agreement, is properly a matter for a specific government policy decision and not for an administrative decision on the part of the corporation.
My remarks provoked the minister to suggest that I was engaged in a special pleading; that I simply wanted the plant in my constituency rather than in someone else's; that I was prepared to sacrifice the best interests of 6,000 fishermen on the altar of 120 to 150 jobs for Selkirk. First of all let me disabuse the minister of the assumption that Selkirk is the largest centre in my riding. As a matter of fact, better than 66 per cent of the voters in the constituency of Selkirk live in metropolitan Winnipeg, the site currently favoured for the location of the plant. Rather, my support for the Selkirk location is based upon the following four considerations. First, 150 new jobs in Winnipeg, while desirable, would have only a marginal effect on that city's economy, whereas the loss of a similar number of jobs in the town of Selkirk through the relocation of the plant would represent an economic disaster of major proportions; second, the relocation of the plant would have a powerfully adverse effect upon the ARDA-FRED development plans for the entire interlake area, based as they are upon agriculture and the fisheries; third, the relocation of the plant would involve the loss of compatible employment for the Indians and Metis of the interlake area. Here it is interesting to note that at any given time 40 per cent to 60 per cent of the employees of the Selkirk plant are of Indian or Metis descent and that the income of at least one entire Indian village is almost totally dependent upon the existence of the plant in Selkirk. Fourth, the movement of the plant to Winnipeg represents one more step in the direction of the concentration of the industry and the population of Manitoba in metropolitan Winnipeg, a step which is socially undesirable both from the point of view of increased urban congestion and from the point of view of a further decline in the vitality and quality of life in the rural and semirural regions of the province.
The minister also charged, as I noted earlier, that I was willing to sacrifice the economic well-being of 6,000 fishermen distributed throughout the west and northwest in order to keep 120 to 150 jobs in my constituency. Far from it. My argument was that the economic benefits of the Winnipeg location had not been proved, and that even if there were an economic disadvantage to the Selkirk
June 25, 1970

site, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion grant which has been offered more than offset it.
Moreover, I argued that it was a case of weighing the certain harm to the economic development potential of the entire interlake region of Manitoba against a largely hypothetical disadvantage to the fishermen. In respect of the economic consideration let me quote from a brief prepared by the Manitoba Department of Industry and Commerce, prepared for presentation to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation in early June. It states in part as follows:
The location cost comparison conducted by the Manitoba Department of Industry and Commerce based on information provided by the FFMC, and accepted by the FFMC, concludes that economic factors favour a Selkirk location. Considering the minimum grant differential offered by the federal Department of Regional Economic Expansion the cost saving in Selkirk is $17,752 per year over the optimum Metro Winnipeg site which is St. Boniface. This annual saving is equivalent to an initial amortized capital difference of $151,123.
It continues:
Within the past week it was revealed by the FFMC that the grant differential offered by DREE may be as much as 40 per cent higher than the figure used in the Dept, of I & C study. This larger grant, equal to $5,000 per job, would result in a total cost advantage to Selkirk of $52,287 per year or an initial saving of $445,123.
Even without considering the Department of Regional Economic Expansion grants, the hypothetical advantage of St. Boniface over Selkirk could only amount to a total of $34,048 per year, the brief indicated. The Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation's case for a Winnipeg as opposed to a Selkirk location for the new plant would now seem to be based upon considerations of cost and speed of transportation vis-a-vis Winnipeg and Selkirk, and upon the hypothetical assumption that the movement of fish will shift from truck to rail. Such an assumption, I suggest, is highly questionable but I do not propose to debate it. Rather, I would refer to the offer from the government of Manitoba in response to the Minister of Fisheries' (Mr. Davis) demand that the government "put up or shut up".
The government of Manitoba has now indicated that in order to assure a Selkirk location it is prepared "to accept the actual costs of transhipping if it exceeds the amount defrayed by DREE." In short, the government
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion of Manitoba is prepared to cover any increased costs of shipping that might be incurred by the corporation through locating in Selkirk. I suggest that this offer removes the last remaining objection to a Selkirk location. I would therefore earnestly entreat the minister to use his power and influence to ensure that the processing plant remains in Selkirk. The social advantages of such a course are manifestly obvious and any potential economic obstacle has now been removed.
